title: Vocabulary: paraphrase power for Reading and Listening
status: Owner approved v1.1.0 on 2026-10-26; teacher release to all eligible schools (optional vocabulary lesson)
rights: Original Brains Heist LLC instructional material, AI-assisted. Passages, people and data are fictional and created for practice. Not official IELTS material. Human editorial and classroom review recommended.
prerequisites: Lesson 5 (Listening distractors and paraphrases) or Lesson 6 (Reading for specific information).
Learners have met TRUE/FALSE/NOT GIVEN at least once.
Pitched at learners aiming for Band 6.5-7.5 who lose marks because questions use different words from the text.

objectives.text: Recognise 14 high-frequency IELTS paraphrase sets quickly and accurately (for example inadequate = not enough, predominantly = mainly).
Detect near-miss paraphrases that change quantity, certainty, time or cause.
Paraphrase a Writing task question accurately in an introduction, without copying or changing its meaning.

levels.foundation: Use the word bank throughout; for each reading answer, underline the matching words in the passage before deciding.
levels.core: Close the word bank after the first stage; name the paraphrase that decided each reading answer.
levels.extension: For each wrong option in the first task, say exactly what it changes (quantity, certainty, time or cause).
levels.high_band: In the writing task, paraphrase each question using different structures as well as different words (for example a noun phrase instead of a clause).

word_bank.meaning: become smaller in number or amount
word_bank.example: Visitor numbers declined = fewer people visited.

word_bank.meaning: large in size, amount or importance
word_bank.example: a substantial increase = a large rise

word_bank.item: approximately / roughly / in the region of
word_bank.meaning: close to, but not exactly, a number

word_bank.example: Cars are prohibited = cars are banned.

word_bank.meaning: no longer used because something newer exists
word_bank.example: obsolete equipment = equipment nobody uses now

word_bank.meaning: not enough, or not good enough

word_bank.example: reluctant to invest = did not want to invest

word_bank.item: predominantly / mainly / for the most part
word_bank.example: predominantly female = most, not all, were women
acquire a skill = learn a skill
Consequently, prices rose = so prices went up.
vital supplies = supplies people cannot do without

word_bank.meaning: lasting only for a limited time
word_bank.example: an interim measure = a step taken until a permanent one is ready

word_bank.item: the elderly / older people / senior citizens
word_bank.example: services for the elderly = help for older residents

word_bank.meaning: so small that it hardly matters
word_bank.example: a negligible effect = almost no effect

stages.title: Opening challenge: same idea, different words
stages.student: Decide which learner reasoned best before the reveal.
stages.teacher: Learners vote. Reveal the comments. Stress that IELTS questions rarely repeat the text's words, and that small words decide the answer.
stages.say: Match the idea, then check every detail: amount, certainty, time and cause.
stages.check: Learners can say why Learner A and Learner C are wrong.

stages.title: Word bank: paraphrase sets
stages.student: Cover the meaning column. Explain each set to a partner and give one example sentence.
stages.teacher: Drill stress (con-SID-er-a-ble, pre-DOM-in-ant-ly, in-dis-PEN-sa-ble). Point out word families: decline (verb/noun), substantial(ly).
stages.say: Learn sets of words, not single words: the test will use the one you did not expect.
stages.check: Pairs can give a partner word for ten sets with the meaning column covered.

stages.title: Exact or near-miss?
stages.student: Choose the sentence that means exactly the same as the original. Every option is a correct English sentence.
stages.teacher: Seven minutes, word bank closed for core and above. In the reveal, ask what each wrong option changes.
stages.say: A paraphrase keeps the same amount, certainty, time and cause.
stages.check: Learners identify the change in at least two distractors per question.

stages.title: Reading: repair cafés
stages.student: Answer the ten questions in twelve minutes. Underline the words in the passage that mean the same as each question.
stages.teacher: Twelve minutes, then reveal. For each answer, ask learners to name the paraphrase pair that decided it.
stages.say: Locate the idea, then test every word in the question against the passage.
stages.check: Learners quote evidence for every answer and explain both NOT GIVEN answers.

stages.title: Paraphrase the question
stages.student: Write the three introductions. Change the words and, where you can, the structure; never change the meaning.
stages.teacher: Twelve minutes, no model visible. Note learners who copy more than four words in a row from a question.
stages.say: Copied words do not count towards your word total in the real test, and changed meaning loses Task marks.
stages.check: Every learner finishes at least two introductions.

stages.title: Compare with the model and check
stages.student: Compare with the model. Use the checklist to find one place where your paraphrase changed the meaning, and fix it.
stages.teacher: Ask two learners to read an introduction aloud; the class says whether the meaning has changed.
stages.say: The model is illustrative, not a target band.
stages.check: Each learner makes one correction to their own work.

stages.title: Exit ticket and homework
stages.student: Complete the exit ticket and note the homework.
stages.teacher: Collect exit tickets; note which sets are still unknown.
stages.say: After every practice test, add the paraphrases you missed to your own list.
stages.check: Every learner writes three paraphrase sets from memory.

blocks.title: Same idea, different words
blocks.mode: Opening challenge; learners decide before the reveal
blocks.instructions: Passage: 'Over the past decade, the number of visitors to the museum has declined substantially.' Statement: 'Far fewer people visit the museum than ten years ago.' Three learners answered TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN. Whose reasoning is best?

examples.label: Learner A
examples.text: NOT GIVEN, because the words 'fewer people visit' are not in the passage.
examples.comment: Wrong: IELTS statements are almost always paraphrased. 'Declined substantially' means 'far fewer'.

examples.label: Learner B
examples.text: TRUE, because 'declined' = 'fewer', 'substantially' = 'far', and 'over the past decade' = 'than ten years ago'.
examples.comment: Best: every part of the statement is matched to the passage by meaning, including the amount and the time.

examples.label: Learner C
examples.text: FALSE, because the passage says 'substantially', and the statement says 'far', which is stronger.
examples.comment: Wrong: 'substantially' and 'far' express a similar large amount. Only a clear contradiction makes a statement FALSE.

blocks.title: Exact or near-miss?
blocks.mode: Controlled practice; word bank closed for core and above
blocks.instructions: Choose the sentence, A, B, C or D, that means exactly the same as the original. All the options are correct English; only one keeps the original meaning.

items.prompt: Original: 'The scheme was used predominantly by students.'
items.evidence: predominantly = mainly, not exclusively
items.reason: A says 'only' (all); B says half; D reverses the meaning.
options: A  Only students used the scheme.
B  About half of the scheme's users were students.
C  Most of the people who used the scheme were students.
D  Students made little use of the scheme.

items.prompt: Original: 'Prices may decline next year.'
items.evidence: may = possibility, not certainty
items.reason: A and D are certain; C changes the time to the past.
options: A  Prices will fall next year.
B  It is possible that prices will drop next year.
C  Prices fell last year.
D  Prices are certain to stay the same next year.

items.prompt: Original: 'The road has been closed as an interim measure.'
items.evidence: interim = temporary, until a permanent solution
items.reason: B makes it permanent; C adds a reason that is not given; D changes the time.
options: A  The road has been shut for a limited period until a longer-term solution is found.
B  The road has been closed permanently.
C  The road has been closed because it was dangerous.
D  The road will be closed in the near future.

items.prompt: Original: 'Funding was inadequate to complete the project.'
items.evidence: inadequate = not enough
items.reason: A says there was no money at all; B says the project was finished; C blames the cost of materials, which is not stated.
options: A  There was no money at all for the project.
B  The project was completed despite limited funds.
C  The project failed because materials became more expensive.
D  There was not enough money to finish the project.

items.prompt: Original: 'Residents were reluctant to accept the new parking rules.'
items.evidence: reluctant = unwilling, but not necessarily refusing
items.reason: A says they refused; C reverses the attitude; D changes who was unwilling.
options: A  Residents refused to accept the new parking rules.
B  Residents did not really want to accept the new parking rules.
C  Residents welcomed the new parking rules.
D  The council was unwilling to introduce new parking rules.

items.prompt: Original: 'The effect of the new law on crime was negligible.'
items.evidence: negligible = so small that it hardly matters
items.reason: A and B say the law had a large effect; D says the effect is unknown.
options: A  The new law led to a sharp fall in crime.
B  The new law caused crime to increase considerably.
C  The new law made almost no difference to crime.
D  Nobody knows whether the new law affected crime.

items.prompt: Original: 'Consequently, the library extended its opening hours.'
items.evidence: consequently = as a result (of what was said before)
items.reason: B adds a specific reason that is not in the original; C changes the time; D reverses the change.
options: A  As a result, the library opened for longer.
B  The library opened for longer because students complained.
C  The library will soon open for longer.
D  As a result, the library reduced its opening hours.

items.prompt: Original: 'Senior citizens make up roughly a third of the town's population.'
items.evidence: senior citizens = older people; roughly a third = about 33%
items.reason: A changes the group; B makes the figure exact; C changes the proportion to a majority.
options: A  About a third of the town's residents are children.
B  Exactly one in three residents is over sixty-five.
C  Most of the town's residents are elderly.
D  Approximately 33 per cent of the town's residents are older people.

blocks.title: Reading: repair cafés
blocks.mode: Timed practice under test-like conditions: twelve minutes, no dictionary
blocks.instructions: Questions 1-6: Do the following statements agree with the information in the passage? Write TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN. Questions 7-10: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

stimulus.title: Repair cafés
paragraphs: Over the past decade, repair cafés have appeared in a substantial number of towns and cities across Europe. At these events, which are usually held once a month in community halls or libraries, volunteers with technical skills help residents to mend household items such as lamps, bicycles, clothing and small electrical appliances. Visitors do not pay for the service, although many leave a voluntary donation towards the cost of tools and refreshments.

The organisers' central argument is that a large proportion of discarded products are not genuinely beyond repair. Instead, they are thrown away because their owners lack the tools, the knowledge or simply the confidence to attempt a repair themselves. Visitors are therefore expected to stay with their item and take part in the repair rather than leave it to be collected later, on the principle that people who have fixed something once are more likely to try again at home.

Data collected by one national network suggest that roughly two thirds of the items brought in are successfully repaired on the day. Those that cannot be fixed are frequently electronic devices for which spare parts are no longer manufactured, or products that have been glued or sealed in a way that prevents them from being opened without being damaged. The network has used these records to argue that manufacturers should be required to make products easier to dismantle, so that worn components can be replaced rather than the whole product being discarded.

Surveys of visitors indicate that attendance is predominantly made up of people over the age of fifty, many of whom grew up at a time when mending clothes and appliances was a routine part of household life. Organisers are keen to attract younger residents, and several cafés now run sessions specifically for students, although it is not yet clear whether these have changed the overall age profile.

Funding remains a persistent difficulty. Most cafés depend on small grants from local councils, which are frequently inadequate to cover the cost of room hire and specialist equipment, and a number have consequently been forced to reduce the frequency of their events or close altogether. Volunteer numbers are also a concern, since a small number of experienced repairers often carry much of the workload, and organisers worry about what will happen when they are no longer able to take part.

Manufacturers' responses have been mixed. Some have begun to publish repair manuals and sell spare parts directly to the public. Others have been reluctant to do so, arguing that untrained people could damage products or injure themselves, particularly when working with electrical items. In several countries, however, new legislation now obliges manufacturers of certain appliances to make spare parts available for a fixed number of years after a product is withdrawn from sale.

items.prompt: People who bring items to a repair café are charged a small fee for each repair.
items.evidence: Visitors do not pay for the service
items.reason: The repairs are free; donations are voluntary, not a charge.

items.prompt: Visitors are encouraged to help fix their own belongings.
items.evidence: Visitors are therefore expected to stay with their item and take part in the repair
items.reason: 'Help fix their own belongings' paraphrases 'take part in the repair'.

items.prompt: Electrical appliances take longer to repair than clothing.
items.evidence: Both are mentioned, but repair times are never compared.
items.reason: The passage lists types of item but gives no information about how long repairs take.

items.prompt: Around sixty-six per cent of the objects brought to the events are fixed during the same visit.
items.evidence: roughly two thirds of the items brought in are successfully repaired on the day
items.reason: 'Around sixty-six per cent' = 'roughly two thirds'; 'during the same visit' = 'on the day'.

items.prompt: Special sessions for students have clearly increased the proportion of young visitors.
items.evidence: it is not yet clear whether these have changed the overall age profile
items.reason: The passage says the effect is not yet clear, which contradicts 'clearly increased'.

items.prompt: Repair cafés in rural villages are more successful than those in large cities.
items.evidence: Towns and cities are mentioned, but villages are not, and no type of location is compared.
items.reason: The passage gives no information comparing cafés in different kinds of place.

items.prompt: According to the organisers, many products are thrown away because
items.evidence: they are thrown away because their owners lack the tools, the knowledge or simply the confidence
items.reason: 'Do not feel able to repair them' paraphrases a lack of tools, knowledge or confidence; A and B are not claimed; D is the opposite of the organisers' argument.
options: A  replacement products have become cheaper.
B  modern products are designed to break quickly.
C  their owners do not feel able to repair them.
D  they are genuinely impossible to repair.

items.prompt: Which kind of item does the passage say is often impossible to repair?
items.evidence: Those that cannot be fixed are frequently electronic devices for which spare parts are no longer manufactured
items.reason: 'Parts are no longer made' paraphrases 'spare parts are no longer manufactured'.
options: A  electronic devices whose spare parts are no longer produced
B  clothing made from synthetic materials
C  bicycles that are more than twenty years old
D  products that were bought online

items.prompt: What does the passage say about volunteers?
items.evidence: a small number of experienced repairers often carry much of the workload
items.reason: 'A few people do most of the work' paraphrases this; A, B and C are not stated.
options: A  Most of them are under the age of fifty.
B  They are paid from council grants.
C  They must hold a formal qualification.
D  A few experienced people do much of the work.

items.prompt: What is said about the attitude of manufacturers?
items.evidence: Manufacturers' responses have been mixed.
items.reason: Some publish manuals and sell parts; others are reluctant. 'They do not all respond in the same way' paraphrases 'mixed'.
options: A  They have all opposed repair cafés.
B  They have not all responded in the same way.
C  They are now required to provide repair training.
D  They support repair cafés financially.

blocks.title: Paraphrase the question
blocks.mode: Independent classroom application after modelling; not a full Writing task
blocks.prompt: Write an introduction for each task below. Paraphrase the question in your own words (do not copy more than three words in a row) and, for the Task 2 questions, add a one-sentence position or outline. (1) Task 1: The graph below shows the number of international students enrolled at universities in three countries between 2000 and 2020. (2) Task 2: Some people think that the government should provide free public transport. To what extent do you agree or disagree? (3) Task 2: In many countries, the number of people living alone is increasing. What are the reasons for this, and is it a positive or negative development?
blocks.conditions: 12 minutes, independent. No model visible. Record word-bank use.
blocks.support: Change at least two things in each question: words (number of people = proportion of residents), structure (a clause becomes a noun phrase), or order. Keep the time period, places and question parts exactly.
blocks.extension: Use a different structure in each introduction, for example 'There has been a rise in ...' or 'Whether ... is a matter of debate.'
blocks.high_band: In introduction 3, answer both parts of the question in one clear sentence.
blocks.model_label: Illustrative classroom model for discussion only. Not a certified band answer.
blocks.model:
(1) The line graph illustrates how many overseas students were studying at universities in three different countries over a twenty-year period, from 2000 to 2020.

(2) It is sometimes argued that public transport should be paid for entirely by the state, so that passengers travel without charge. While I accept that this would benefit some groups, I largely disagree, because the cost would ultimately fall on taxpayers and could reduce investment in the quality of services.

(3) A growing proportion of the population in many nations now lives in single-person households. This trend can be explained by rising incomes and changing attitudes to marriage, and in my view it is largely positive, although it may increase loneliness among older people.
checklist: Task Response: Does each introduction keep every part of the question (time, places, both questions)?
Lexical Resource: Have you avoided copying more than three words in a row?
Lexical Resource: Is the meaning exactly the same (no change in amount, time or cause)?
Coherence and Cohesion: Does each Task 2 introduction end with a clear position or outline?

blocks.title: Homework: paraphrase in context
blocks.mode: Homework; checked at the start of the next lesson
blocks.instructions: Questions 1-3: Write a word-bank word or phrase (no more than THREE words) that could replace the words in brackets without changing the meaning. Questions 4-6: Paraphrase each sentence. Keep the meaning exactly the same and do not copy more than three words in a row.

items.prompt: Support for the plan was (mostly but not entirely) among younger voters.
items.evidence: predominantly = mostly, not entirely
items.reason: 'Mainly' or 'for the most part' are also correct.

items.prompt: The software has become (no longer used because something newer exists).
items.evidence: obsolete = outdated
items.reason: 'Outdated' is also correct.

items.prompt: Clean water is (absolutely necessary) for public health.
items.evidence: essential / vital / indispensable
items.reason: Any of the three is correct.

items.prompt: Paraphrase: 'The number of people cycling to work has risen considerably since 2010.'
items.answer: Since 2010, there has been a substantial increase in the number of commuters who travel by bicycle.
items.evidence: considerably = substantially; cycling to work = commuting by bicycle
items.reason: Accept any accurate paraphrase that keeps 'since 2010', a large increase and the idea of travelling to work.

items.prompt: Paraphrase: 'Many older residents are unwilling to use online banking.'
items.answer: A large number of senior citizens are reluctant to bank online.
items.evidence: unwilling = reluctant; older residents = senior citizens
items.reason: Accept any accurate paraphrase; 'many' must not become 'most' or 'all'.

items.prompt: Paraphrase: 'Because the grant was too small, the festival was cancelled.'
items.answer: The grant was insufficient; consequently, the festival had to be cancelled.
items.evidence: too small = insufficient/inadequate; because = consequently
items.reason: Accept any accurate paraphrase that keeps the cause and the result.

exit_ticket: Three paraphrase sets I can now recognise:
One near-miss that tricked me today, and what it changed:
What I will do when a word in a question is not in the passage:
homework: Complete the paraphrase tasks on the homework sheet.
After your next practice test, add every paraphrase you missed to your own list, with the passage word and the question word side by side.
delayed_followup: In Lesson 13 (advanced TRUE/FALSE/NOT GIVEN) or Lesson 18 (timed Reading), check whether learners name the paraphrase that decided each answer. Record it as a later observation.

blocks.title: Fresh check: exact or near-miss?
blocks.instructions: Choose the sentence, A, B, C or D, that means exactly the same as the original.

items.prompt: Original: 'Smoking is prohibited throughout the building.'
items.evidence: prohibited = banned; throughout = everywhere in
items.reason: A limits the ban to some areas; C changes a rule into advice; D changes the time.
options: A  Smoking is banned in some parts of the building.
B  Smoking is not allowed anywhere in the building.
C  People are advised not to smoke in the building.
D  Smoking will soon be banned in the building.

items.prompt: Original: 'Staff numbers fell substantially after the merger.'
items.evidence: fell substantially = dropped considerably
items.reason: A reverses the direction; B makes the change small; C changes the time.
options: A  The company employed many more people after the merger.
B  Staff numbers fell slightly after the merger.
C  Staff numbers had fallen before the merger.
D  The number of employees dropped considerably after the merger.

items.prompt: Original: 'The plan was hesitantly approved by the committee.'
items.evidence: hesitantly approved = approved, but without enthusiasm
items.reason: A and D say it was not approved; B reverses the attitude.
options: A  The committee rejected the plan.
B  The committee approved the plan enthusiastically.
C  The committee approved the plan, although with some doubts.
D  The committee has not yet decided about the plan.

items.prompt: Original: 'The cost of the repairs was negligible.'
items.evidence: negligible = very small
items.reason: B and D make the cost large; C says the cost is unknown.
options: A  The repairs cost very little.
B  The repairs were extremely expensive.
C  Nobody knows how much the repairs cost.
D  The repairs cost more than expected.

blocks.title: Fresh check: community orchards
blocks.instructions: Do the statements agree with the information in the passage? Write TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN.

stimulus.title: Community orchards
paragraphs: Community orchards, in which local residents plant and look after fruit trees on shared land, have become considerably more common in British towns over the past twenty years. Most are established on land that would otherwise be unused, such as the edges of parks or the grounds of schools and hospitals.

Volunteers are predominantly retired people and families with young children. Because many sites are leased on a temporary basis, groups are often hesitant to plant slow-growing varieties, some of which take several years to produce a crop. Researchers have found that people who take part report lower levels of stress, although it is not clear whether gardening itself, or the social contact it involves, is responsible.

items.prompt: There are far more community orchards in British towns than there were two decades ago.
items.evidence: have become considerably more common in British towns over the past twenty years
items.reason: 'Far more' paraphrases 'considerably more common'; 'two decades' = 'twenty years'.

items.prompt: Most volunteers are teenagers.
items.evidence: Volunteers are predominantly retired people and families with young children
items.reason: The main groups are retired people and young families, not teenagers.

items.prompt: Some groups avoid planting trees that take a long time to bear fruit.
items.evidence: groups are often hesitant to plant slow-growing varieties, some of which take several years to produce a crop
items.reason: 'Avoid' paraphrases 'are hesitant to plant'; 'bear fruit' = 'produce a crop'.

items.prompt: Researchers have shown that the physical work of gardening is the cause of lower stress.
items.evidence: it is not clear whether gardening itself, or the social contact it involves, is responsible
items.reason: 'Have shown' is contradicted by 'it is not clear'.
